blocks.text: Figure 3.12 shows a satellite going round the Earth in a circular path. Let the mass of the satellite be mₛ and v is its orbital speed. The mass of the Earth is M and r represents the radius of the orbit. A centripetal force mₛv²/r is required to hold the satellite in the orbit. This force is provided by the gravitational force of attraction between the Earth and the satellite. Equating the gravitational force to the required centripetal force, we have

blocks.alt: The Earth at the centre of a circular orbit. A satellite on the orbit is joined to the Earth's centre by a line carrying an arrow F towards the Earth, and an arrow from the satellite points along the tangent to the orbit. Labels: Earth, Satellite, F.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.12: A satellite going round the Earth in a circular orbit (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.12).

blocks.text_alt: G mₛ M / r² = mₛ v² / r

blocks.text: This shows that the mass of the satellite is unimportant in describing the satellite's orbit. Thus, any satellite orbiting at distance r from the Earth's centre must have the orbital speed given by Eq. 3.15. Any speed less than this will bring the satellite tumbling back to the Earth.
The moment you switch on your mobile phone, your location can be tracked immediately by global positioning system.
blocks.title: Tidbits
Example 3.4
blocks.problem: An Earth satellite is in circular orbit at distance of 384,000 km from the Earth's surface. What is its period of one revolution in days? Take mass of the Earth M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and its radius R = 6400 km.
steps: Using v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² × 6 × 10²⁴ kg / 390400 km)

blocks.text: √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ ÷ 3.904 × 10⁸ m) = √(1.025 × 10⁶ m² s⁻²) = 1.01 × 10³ m s⁻¹, so v = 1.01 km s⁻¹; the printed 1.025 is the value under the square root (in 10⁶ m² s⁻²). The period uses the orbit radius: T = 2πr/v = 2 × 3.14 × 390400 km ÷ 1.01 km s⁻¹ = 2.42 × 10⁶ s = 28.0 days.
